title.en: Dawn's-Heart and the Lynx: The Star Husband's Wife
title.zh: 晨心星與天貓：星夫之妻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\ko-g\nuih-tara, wife of the Dawn's-Heart Star, Jupiter'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §25

summary.en: Jupiter, the Dawn's-Heart star, married the Lynx, then a beautiful woman; the hyena, jealous, bewitched her with poisoned 'Bushman rice' so she became a lioness, and by night took her place in the hut. The star's eyes glowed like fires as he came home; he stabbed at the impostor, missed, and his wife, enticed from the reeds and stripped of her lion skin, could never eat Bushman rice again — she became the lynx that eats meat.
summary.zh: 晨心星（木星）娶天貓——其時為美婦；土狼妒之，以毒「桑人之米」巫化其為母獅，夜間代居其位。星目如火歸家；擲矛擊偽者不中；其妻自蘆葦被誘出，剝獅皮復為人——然終不復食桑人之米，遂為食肉之獰貓。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his mother |xabbi-an) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Dawn's-Heart (Jupiter) had a beautiful wife of the early race and a younger sister-in-law, \xe-dde-yoe, who carried the digging-stick and minded the child. The Dawn's-Heart buried his child under the leaves of an edible root, hoping his wife would find it; other animals and birds arrived first and each proposed herself as mother, and the child mocked them until it recognized its own mother. Among the insulted animals were the Jackal and the Hyena, who plotted revenge.

They bewitched the Lynx with poisoned 'Bushman rice' — so-called ants' eggs — and she was transformed into a lioness. In the dark the Hyena tried to take her place in the hut when the Dawn's-Heart returned; but he noticed that the woman who sat with her back toward him was not his wife, and his sister-in-law told him of the imposture. He seized his assegai and stabbed at the place where the Hyena had been sitting; she sprang out, trod burning her foot in the fire, and fled, leaving the ornaments she had worn.

The bewitched wife had hidden in the reeds. Her sister called her at morning and again near sunset, and each time she came out to suckle the child, saying that her thinking-strings were falling, that she was forgetting. At last the sister brought goats, and the people hid around; when the wife sprang from the reeds to the goats, the Dawn's-Heart caught her and all the people held her fast. They cut open the goats, took out the contents of the stomachs and anointed her, rubbing off the lion hair; she asked that the hair on the tips of her ears be left, 'for in that manner I shall come to hear.'

She became a fair woman again; but because she had been bewitched by Bushman rice she could no longer eat it. She was changed into the lynx who eats meat, and the Dawn's-Heart, going home from hunting ever after, walked with an arrow on the bow and the assegai stuck in the ground, his eyes large like fires — for the hyenas had poisoned his wife, and his heart would never be quiet again. The discourses attached to this myth are long: the Dawn's-Heart talks to his daughter of their own history, of the lynx-mother, of the sun, moon and stars, and of the habits of lions and Bushmen, running at last into a whole account of the jackals' doings; and the fugitive hyena, her foot burnt in the fire, is followed home through long speeches with her mother and father about suitable marriages. In the second long piece the narrative of about seventy-two columns is followed by the hyena family's talk. The stars keep the story in the sky: Jupiter walks as the only Dawn's-Heart when his heart-daughter is swallowed, and precedes the Dawn's-Heart-child; the identification with Regulus was made at the Cape Observatory in the 1870s, on the narrators' pointing. The myth also fixes Bushman hut etiquette — the wife sits facing her husband, and the stranger who sits with her back to the door is the one to be suspected — and it teaches that poisoned food given in beauty is the most dangerous gift of all, for the Lynx ate what was offered to her and never tasted Bushman-rice again.

functions: Explains the lynx's diet and the tufts on its ears.
Charter for the woman 'sitting with her back' etiquette of the hut.
Links the planet Jupiter and his child-star to a domestic tragedy of the early race.

variants.summary: A long discourse from the Dawn's-Heart to his daughter, treating their history, the lynx-mother, sun, moon and stars, and lions and Bushmen.

variants.name: Hyena flight conversations (B V.-X.)
variants.summary: Long speeches by the fugitive hyena with her burnt foot to her mother and father on suitable marriages.

variants.summary: A short piece with the address of the younger sister to the transformed lioness-wife.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: 19th-century colonial-era collection; identify star names as given by the narrators and the Royal Observatory, not as astronomical fact.

passages.text: And \kó-g\nuin-tdra exclaimed, she said to her younger sister: 'Thou shalt leave this |haken alone; I will be the one who eats it. For, thou art the one who shalt take care of the child. For, this |haken, its smell is not nice.' Therefore, as \kó-g\nuin-tdra sat, eating the |haken, the ornaments of themselves came off.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 86 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Dawn's-Heart ran to the hyena; he took aim (with his assegai), he pierced the place where the hyena had been sitting, while the hyena sprang out, she trod, burning herself in the fire, while she sprang away; while the ornaments remained at the place where she had been sitting... And the Dawn's-Heart scolded his younger sister-in-law, why was it that his younger sister-in-law had not quickly told him about it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 92-93 (public domain).

passages.text: They cut the goats open, they took out the contents of the stomach, they anointed \kó-g\nuin-tdra with the contents of the stomachs. They, taking hold, rubbed off the hair from her skin. Therefore, when she sat down, she said: 'Ye must, pulling, leave the hair on the tips of my ears; for, in that manner I shall come to hear; for, I do not feel as if I should hear.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 95-96 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§25): the mother of the Dawn's-Heart-child was the Lynx, who was then a beautiful woman; she was bewitched with poisoned Bushman rice and transformed into a lioness; her brothers pulled off the lion skin so that she became a fair woman again; but, in consequence of having been bewitched by Bushman rice, she could no longer eat that, and was changed into a lynx who ate meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 (Bleek archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §25; Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), p. 96 extract

summary.en: The Dawn's-Heart star has a daughter, his 'heart': he swallows her, walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart, and when she is grown spits her out again. She becomes another female Dawn's-Heart and spits out another child which follows the pair — the recurring star-child that follows Jupiter across the sky.
summary.zh: 晨心星有一女，是其「心」：吞之，獨行為唯一晨心星；及長復吐出。女遂為另一晨心星，再吐新女隨行——即天上恆隨木星之 repeat 星子。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San star lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§25): the Dawn's-Heart (the star Jupiter) has a daughter, who is identified with some neighbouring star preceding Jupiter. Her name is the Dawn's-Heart-child, and her relation to her father is somewhat mysterious. He calls her 'my heart', he swallows her, then walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart Star, and, when she is grown up, he spits her out again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She then herself becomes another female Dawn's-Heart, and spits out another Dawn's-Heart-child, which follows the male and female Dawn's-Heart. The Dawn's-Heart hid his first child under the leaves of an edible root, where he thought that his wife would come and find it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.

title.en: The Son of the Wind Rolls the Ball

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Son of the Wind'

summary.en: The Wind's child rolls a ball to |na-ka-ti, calling his name, but no one knows his; his mother warns |na-ka-ti to utter the name only when the hut is screened, and then run in — for the Wind will blow him away. |na-ka-ti shouts '\erriten-\kuan-\kuan!' and the storm flattens the boy and drives the huts apart; only the Wind's mother can raise him up. The Wind lies when it blows hard, and stands when it is still; and the Wind was once a man who became a bird that dwells in a mountain hole.
summary.zh: 風子滾球喚名，無人知其名；母囑：俟屏帳成方可呼其名，呼畢速入屋，防風捲走。名既出，颶風立至，掀屋倒童；唯風母扶之起。風猛吹時乃「臥」，靜時乃「立」；風本為人，化鳥棲山穴。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
The (son of the) Wind was formerly still. And he rolled (a ball) to 
a-ka-ti. He exclaimed: 'O 
a-ka-ti! There it goes!' And 
a-ka-ti exclaimed: 'O comrade! There it goes!' because 
a-ka-ti felt that he did not know his (the other one's) name.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 101 (public domain).

passages.text: His mother exclaimed: 'I will not utter to thee comrade's name. For, thou shalt wait; that father may first shelter for us the hut... And thou shalt, when I have uttered for thee comrade's name, thou must scamper away, thou must run home, that thou mayest come into the hut, whilst thou dost feel that the wind would blow thee away.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 102-103 (public domain).

passages.text: He beheld that his father had finished sheltering the hut, then he exclaimed: 'There it goes! O \erriten-\kuan-\kuan! There it goes! O \gau-\gaubu-ti! There it goes!' And he scampered away, he ran home; while the other one began to lean over, and the other one fell down. He lay kicking violently upon the vlei. Therefore, the people's huts vanished away, the wind blew, breaking their sheltering bushes, together with the huts.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 104-105 (public domain).

passages.text: His mother came out of the hut; his mother came, grasping (him), to raise him up... Therefore, the wind became still... Therefore, we who are Bushmen, we are wont to say: 'The wind seems to be lying down, for, it does not gently blow.' The Wind (the Wind's son) was formerly a man. He became a bird. And he was flying... he dwelt in a mountain (that is, in a mountain hole).
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 106-107 (public domain).

title.zh: 卡加拉與哈烏奴雷電相鬥

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\kagara and \haunu, who fought each other with Lightning'

summary.en: \kagara the little bird-man rescues his sister from her husband \haunu, a Rain sorcerer. The brother-in-law sneezes blood and lightens at them; \kagara fends off the strokes and at last strikes back with the black lightning that kills, felling \haunu, who lies thundering. The grandmothers said these two fight in the east whenever the clouds stand like a mountain.
summary.zh: 小鳥人卡加拉自其妹夫——雨巫哈烏奴——處奪回妹妹。妹夫噴血閃電擊之；卡加拉揮臂格擋，終以「黑雷」反擊，擊倒哈烏奴，其臥而雷吼。祖母云：雲聚如山時，此二人在東方相鬥。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his grandmother ≠kammi) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They formerly, \kagara formerly went to fetch his younger sister, he went to take her away; he went to take her away from \haunu; and he took (her) back to her parents. \haunu gave chase to his brother-in-law, he passed along behind the hill. The clouds came, clouds which were unequalled in beauty; they vanished away.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 113 (public domain).

passages.text: Then \haunu sneezed, on account of it; blood poured out of his nostrils; he stealthily lightened at his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law fended him quickly off, his brother-in-law also stealthily lightened at him. He quickly fended off his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law also lightened at him.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 115-116 (public domain).

passages.text: Then he stealthily lightened at his younger sister's husband with black lightning, he, lightening, whisked him up (and carried him to a little distance). His younger sister's husband, in this manner, lay dying; he, in this manner, he thundered, while \kagara bound up his head with the net, he, returning, arrived at home... they went along angry with each other.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 117 (public domain).

passages.text: My grandmothers used to say: '\kagara and his companion are those who fight in the East, he and \haunu.' When the clouds were thick, and the clouds resembled a mountain, then, the clouds were lightening, on account of it. And my grandmothers used to say: 'It is \kagara, with \haunu.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 118 (public domain).

title.en: The Hyena's Revenge on the Grudging Lion

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871 and 1875 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Hyena's Revenge' (two versions); W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §27

summary.en: The lion grudges the hyena his meat; the hyena invites him home, ladles boiling soup into his mouth, jams the hot pot over his head, and beats him dead beneath it. In the second version the lion, who also eats people, has carried off an old woman, and the hyena strikes him down while his head is inside the pot.
summary.zh: 獅吝於予土狼肉；土狼邀其至家，以滾湯灌其口，覆熱釜其首，擊殺之。第二版中，食人之獅已擄一老嫗；土狼趁其首入釜時擊斃之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Hyena was the one who went to the Lion's house, then, he deceived the Lion; while he felt that the Lion had acted grudgingly towards him about the quagga's flesh; therefore, the Lion came to the Hyena's house, when the Hyena was boiling there in the Hyena's pot; the Hyena boiled ostrich flesh in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).

passages.text: The Hyena gave soup to the Lion; therefore, the Lion took hold of the pot, while the pot was hot; the Hyena also grasped the pot with his hands; the Hyena said: 'O Lion! Allow me to pour soup into the inside of thy mouth.' The Hyena poured soup into the Lion's mouth; then, he put the mouth of the pot over the Lion's head, while the pot was hot.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).

passages.text: The soup was burning the Lion's eyes; the soup also burned the inside of his mouth. Then, he swallowed hot soup with his throat, he swallowed, causing himself to die with hot soup; he died, while his head was inside the pot. The Hyena took up the Hyena's stick, the Hyena was beating him with the stick, while his head was inside the pot; the Hyena was beating him; the Hyena struck, cleaving the pot asunder.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 123-124 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the second version: the Hyena said 'I am accustomed to pour soup into this child's mouth, I also pour soup into my wife's mouth' — and poured soup into the Lion's mouth, put the Lion's head into the pot, while he felt that he altogether put the Lion's head into the pot; that he might altogether kill the Lion with the soup's heat; and he carried off the old woman on account of it, and struck the Lion down while his head was inside the pot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 126-127; not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Jealous of the Ostrich's Voice

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Lion jealous of the Voice of the Ostrich'

summary.en: The women praise the ostrich's booming; the jealous lion makes them stage a dance, kicks the ostrich's chest as he sings, tears it open, kills him and eats his lungs raw to boom like him. The ostrich's nail decayed from the kick — the scar on its chest is still the lion's nail — and boys must swallow the lungs whole and raw to keep the voice.
summary.zh: 婦人讚鴕鳥鳴聲；獅妒，令婦起舞，趁其鳴時踢其胸膛，撕裂殺之，生吞其肺以效其聲。鴕鳥之爪因踢而朽——胸上疤痕至今乃獅之爪痕。男孩須生吞整肺以存其聲。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Lions conspired together that they might deceive the Ostrich; for, the women were wont, with regard to the Ostrich, they only praised the Ostrich for calling finely; the women did not praise them. And they (the Lions), speaking, said: 'In what manner shall we deceive?'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 128 (public domain).

passages.text: The other Lion answered, he said: 'The ostrich calls with his lungs; therefore, his throat sounds in this manner; his chest's front. Thou dost call with thy mouth; therefore, thou dost not call nicely.' The other Lion answered: 'Ye must make a (game of) \gebbi-ggu, that ye may kill the Ostrich, that ye may take out the Ostrich's lungs... and ye will call, sounding like the Ostrich, when ye have eaten the Ostrich's lungs.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 129-130 (public domain).

passages.text: The Ostrich was still yonder at his house; the Lion called; the women did not applaud the Lion, because they felt that the Lion did not call well... And the Ostrich came; and the Ostrich called, sounding afar. And the women exclaimed: 'I do wish that the Lion called in this manner; for, he sounds as if he had put his tail into his mouth, while the Ostrich calls in a resounding manner.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 130-131 (public domain).

passages.text: He scratched, tearing it. And he called out: 'Is it a thing which calls sweetly?' while he kicked the Ostrich's chest. And the Ostrich also quickly turned back. And the Ostrich also kicked, tearing his chest... My grandfather also gave us the Ostrich's lungs to eat, that we might also resemble the Ostrich... our grandfather spoke... that we should not cook the Ostrich's lungs... we should not chew them, we should swallow them down, while they were whole.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 131-134 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Resurrection of the Ostrich from a Bloody Feather

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1871 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Resurrection of the Ostrich'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §34

summary.en: A hunter kills a male ostrich at its nest; a whirlwind lifts one blood-stained little feather into the sky, drops it into water, and there it becomes ostrich flesh, gains feathers, legs and bone, walks out of the water and returns to his wives as their regained husband. With the Moon and the male ostrich alone of mortal things, he dies and lives again.
summary.zh: 獵者於巢處殺雄鴕；旋風捲血羽上天，落入水中，漸成鴕肉，生羽生足生骨，出水而行，歸其妻為復得之夫。世間凡死不復生者眾，唯月與雄鴕，死而復生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !A!kunta to Bleek and Lloyd, c. 1871; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Bushman kills an ostrich at its eggs and carries the bird home; the wife strips off the bloody short feathers and lays them on the bushes, and the family eats the meat. Then a little whirlwind comes, blows up one small bloodied feather, and lifts it into the sky. It whirls down, falls into the water, becomes wet — and becomes conscious. It lies in the water and becomes ostrich flesh.

In the water it puts on wings and gains its legs; then it walks out of the water and basks on the bank in the sun, for it is still a young ostrich with black quills. It dries its feathers lying on the water's bank, strengthening its feet, hardening its breastbone into bone, eating young bushes, growing. Its little feather it was which became the ostrich, blown up while the wind was a little whirlwind.

It thinks of the place where it scratched its nest; it lets itself grow first, then goes to its old house, to scratch there again, and calls its wives. Because he did die, he will marry three ostrich wives. He roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone; he scratches out a house, and roars to call the females, that they may come to him. He meets them, runs round them, examines their feathers, drives them to the house to lay; he lies inside, guards the eggs against the jackal, and drives the jackal away with his feet — for his children are in the nest.

Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame: this idea of revival through a feather is compared to the Moon's revival; and, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright and do not come to life again — the myth is thus a twin to the Moon's monthly rebirth, and its denial is part of the death-decree world. Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame and its dialogue: the revived bird guards the nest against the attacks of the jackals and hyenas, who are thereby driven to seek for the nest of a she-ostrich who will not be fierce, and who runs away; and the flights of the two cowards are followed in a long, still unfinished dialogue between hyena and jackal. The idea of the revival of a dead male ostrich in and through one of its little feathers is also mentioned elsewhere and is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; whilst, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things are said to die outright and not to come to life again. The hunter who told it had watched the whirlwind lift the plume, and the family stood at the water and saw the flesh come upon it; the myth is thus both an observation of the veld and a resurrection doctrine, for it grants to the ostrich the same monthly immortality as the Moon alone possesses among the old people's dead.

functions: Presents the single great exception to the finality of death.
Explains the male ostrich's nesting behaviour and fierceness at the nest.
Links avian resurrection to lunar resurrection in Bushman eschatology.

variants.name: Short 1875 version (B XII.1171-1213)
variants.summary: Brief outline of the feather's revival, ending with the ostrich guarding the nest and driving off jackals and hyenas.

variants.name: Moon's revival parallel (§16, §34)
variants.summary: The ostrich's return is explicitly compared with the Moon's monthly coming to life again.

W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts

secondary_sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, J. D. 1981. London: Academic Press.
Biesele, M. 1993. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: 19th-century colonial-era collection; presented as archive, not as living authority.

passages.text: The Bushman kills an Ostrich at the Ostrich's eggs; he carries away the Ostrich to the house... A little whirlwind comes to them; it blows up the Ostrich feathers. A little Ostrich feather that has blood upon it, it blows up the little feather into the sky. The little feather falls down out of the sky, it having whirled round falls down, it goes into the water, it becomes wet in the water, it is conscious, it lies in the water, it becomes Ostrich flesh; it gets feathers, it puts on its wings, it gets its legs, while it lies in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 137-138 (public domain).

passages.text: It walks out of the water, it basks in the sun upon the water's edge, because it is still a young Ostrich... He dries (his feathers) lying upon the water's bank, that he may afterwards walk away... He swallows young plants which are small... His little feather it was which became the Ostrich, it was that which the wind blew up, while the wind was a little whirlwind.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 138-140 (public domain).

passages.text: Because his breastbone is bone, he roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone. Then he scratches (out a house)... he roaring calls the Ostrich wives, that the Ostrich wives may come to him... he meets them, that he may run round the females; for he had been dead; he dying left his wives.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 140-141 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§34): a male ostrich is killed and carried home by a Bushman; one of its little feathers, stained with blood, is lifted up by a gentle whirlwind and falls into the water, where it gradually becomes an ostrich; it leaves the water as a young ostrich, grows up, and returns to its wives as their regained husband. This idea of revival is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §34; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vultures, Their Elder Sister, and Her Husband

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Vultures, their elder Sister, and her Husband'

summary.en: The vultures made a woman of the early race their elder sister and lived by her husband's kills; scolded for devouring the springbok, they fly up into the sky and look down, swooping only when game is sighted — and eating in such haste that they must leave the undercut for their sister.
summary.zh: 兀鷲以早期之民女子為姊，賴其夫所獵而活；因吞盡跳羚遭斥，乃飛上天空俯瞰，見獸方落，倉促啄食——須留「腹條」與其姊。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Vultures formerly made their elder sister of a person; they lived with her. They, when their elder sister's husband brought (home) a springbok, they ate up the springbok. And their elder sister's husband cursed them, he scolded at them. And their elder sister took up the skin of the springbok, she singed it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 155 (public domain).

passages.text: They said, this other one said: 'Thou shalt ascend, and then thou must come to tell us what the place seems to be like.'... a Vulture who was a little Vulture girl, she arose, she ascended... she went, disappearing in the sky, they no longer perceived her... Then, their younger sister descended from above out of the sky, she came and sat in the midst of them.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 159-160 (public domain).

passages.text: And she said: 'There is nothing the matter with the place; for, the place is clear. The place is very beautiful; for, I do behold the whole place... the place seems as if we should perceive a springbok, if a springbok were lying under a tree; for the place is very beautiful.' Then, they altogether arose, all of them, they ascended into the sky.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 160-161 (public domain).

passages.text: They said: 'Ye must eat! ye must eat! ye must eat in great haste! for, that accursed man who comes yonder, he could not endure us.' And, they finished the springbok, they flew away, flew heavily away... Their elder sister said: 'Fie! how can ye act in this manner towards me? as if I had been the one who scolded you!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 161-162 (public domain).

title.en: Ddi-≠erreten, the Stone-Headed Man and the Lioness's Children

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Ddi-≠erreten, the Lioness, and the Children'

summary.en: A sick lioness gathers people's children to live with her at the water; Ddi-≠erreten — a man of the early race whose head is stone — sits in her house and sends the children home in batches, telling each that its people's fire burns at the head of this or that ravine. Returning, the lioness finds only the stone head; she bites it, shrieks at her broken teeth, and he goes home, telling her only: 'Our children were not.'
summary.zh: 病母獅聚人童同居水邊；石頭人Ddi-≠erreten入其屋，分批遣童歸家，告以各溝源處其族火所在。母獅歸，唯見石首；咬之，痛呼碎牙。石首唯答：「吾童本非爾有。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten, formerly, when the Lioness was at the water, dipping up water there, Ddi-≠erreten felt that the Lioness was the one who had gathered together the people's children, because the Lioness felt that she was an invalid on account of her chest; therefore, she gathered together the people's children, that the children might live with her, that the children might work for her.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 163-164 (public domain).

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten said: 'O children sitting here! The fire of your people is that which is at the top of the ravine which comes down from the top (of the hill).' Therefore, two children arose, they went away to their own people. Ddi-≠erreten again said... 'The fire of your people is that which is below the top of the ravine which comes down on this side (of the hill).' And three children thus went.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 164-166 (public domain).

passages.text: And the Lioness came from the water, she thus returning came. She came along looking (at the house); she did not perceive the children. And she exclaimed: 'Why do the children not do so to me?... It must be this man who sits at the house; his head resembles Ddi-≠erreten.' And she became angry about it, when she perceived Ddi-≠erreten.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 166-167 (public domain).

passages.text: The Lioness caught hold of his head. She exclaimed 'Growling' to the other one's head. And she exclaimed: 'Oh! Oh dear! my teeth! This must be why this cursed man's big head came to sit in front of my house!' While Ddi-≠erreten said: 'I told thee that our children they were not.'... And he arose, he returned home; while the Lioness sat in anger at her house... she did not a little love the children while she was doing so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 168-169 (public domain).

title.en: The Mason Wasp Shoots His Wife

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Mason Wasp and his Wife'

summary.en: A wife mocks her wasp-husband's thin body when he finally lays down his kaross to shoot a hare; enraged, he turns and shoots her through the breastbone — then cries for his wife as if he had not been the shooter.
summary.zh: 妻譏泥蜂夫之瘦軀，夫怒而轉身射穿其胸骨——隨後呼妻痛哭，若非己射者然。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mason Wasp formerly did thus as he walked along, while (his) wife walked behind him, the wife said: 'O my husband! Shoot for me that hare!'... And the wife said: 'Put down thy kaross! Why is it that thou art not willing to put down thy kaross?' Therefore, the Mason Wasp, walking along, unloosened the strings of the kaross; he put down the kaross.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 171 (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore the wife said: 'Canst thou be like this? This must have been why thou wert not willing to lay down the kaross.' Therefore, the Mason Wasp walked, turning to one side; he aimed at his wife, he shot, hitting the head of the arrow on his wife's breastbone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 171-172 (public domain).

passages.text: And his wife fell down dead on account of it. Then he exclaimed: 'Yi u hihi! O my wife!' (crying) as if he had not been the one to shoot his wife. He cried, that he should have done thus, have shot his wife; his wife died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 172 (public domain).
